tasks.extracted: Meta-analysis of 34 prospective cohort studies published until December 2005 (publication years 1981 to 2005 in Table 2's subgroups): 56 dose-response curves, 1 015 835 participants and 94 533 deaths, each curve against its study's lowest-intake category, which was no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded for 30 curves, and declared no alcohol use (12 curves) or occasional use (14) with former drinkers not excluded. Intake in grams a day; a drink as each study defined it, otherwise 10 g of ethanol (7 studies). The pooled fixed-effect curve was J-shaped: lowest mortality at 6 g a day, about half a drink, relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), a maximum reduction of 19% (17% to 20%); the association with lower mortality was apparent up to 42 g a day (about 4 drinks). A random-effects repeat gave a very similar curve with wider intervals (deviance 879.4 against 154.0), shown only in a figure.

tasks.locator: Abstract and Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 441); Method › Overview; Search strategy for relevant studies (p. 442); Method › Data extraction: Measures of alcohol consumption; Misclassification of former and occasional drinkers as abstainers (p. 443); Method › Criteria for selecting studies of higher or lower quality, items (a) and (b) and last paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 444); Table 1, 'Abstainer biases' (p. 445)
tasks.extracted: 107 prospective cohort studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality from the same group's earlier review: 87 from Stockwell et al. (2016) and 20 added, articles published up to July 31, 2021, English only; 724 risk estimates, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths. Low volume: from one drink a week (more than 1.30 g of ethanol a day) to two drinks a day (less than 25 g); occasional drinkers up to 1 drink of 10 g a week (less than 1.30 g a day); lifetime abstainers never drank one drink; former drinkers had stopped completely by baseline; where a study did not define its drink, national sizes from 8 g (United Kingdom) to 19.75 g (Japan). Studies counted as higher quality had a cohort recruited at a median age of up to 55 and followed to at least 56, with neither former nor occasional drinkers among the abstainers, the two criteria of the preregistered protocol. By world region, 40 studies came from North and Central America, 48 from Europe and Australia and 12 from Asia. Of the 99 studies with low-volume estimates, 18 had neither abstainer bias, 46 both, 27 former drinkers only and 8 occasional drinkers only. The introduction cites evidence that among older cohorts the abstainer group fills up with people who stopped or cut down for health reasons.

tasks.locator: Funding footnote (p. 441); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 446) and 3rd paragraph (p. 446, continuing on p. 447); Conflict-of-Interest Statement (p. 450)
tasks.extracted: Excluding studies with characteristics that predispose to bias gave a higher low-volume estimate than adjusting for those characteristics in the earlier review of the same studies (0.98 against 0.93 in Zhao et al., 2023), which the authors call broadly consistent. They note that neither criterion alone removes all selection biases (the 55-year cut-off is quite high, and abstainer bias cannot be fully corrected unless former drinkers are reallocated to drinking groups) and that more higher-quality studies are needed. Partly funded by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction as part of a contract to assist with Canada's new guidance on alcohol and health; three authors declare previous funding from government alcohol monopolies in Finland, Sweden and Canada for public-health research, two of them past personal fees from these bodies and travel support from IOGT-NTO, a non-governmental organization that advocates against alcohol use. Editors' observation: the six decisive studies are not named and their participants and deaths are not counted in the article, no heterogeneity statistic is reported, and no test of the difference from the lower-quality subgroup is printed; editors' calculation from the printed intervals, treating the two sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03.

An essay, with no methods, data or effect estimates of its own, arguing that Mendelian randomization is an instrumental-variable method subject to confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation and failure of replication; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it must be treated with the caution due to all observational epidemiology; and that it should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis, without the words randomization or causality.

Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common heavy drinking in adolescence and early adulthood, its lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may partly test teenage and young-adult heavy drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.

tasks.locator: Interpreting inconsistency; An appropriate role for GIVA; Summary; Acknowledgements (p. 4); References 17 to 19 (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: The essay says genetic analyses are not immune from inconsistent results and selective publication, and sets the Chinese analysis (its ref. 2), which it says combined genetic and ecological instruments and claimed dose-dependent harm for stroke with no effect on heart attack, against three East Asian reports of higher coronary risk with the ALDH2 variant, which by their titles are a genome-wide association study, an exome-chip meta-analysis and a meta-analysis of gene variants, not instrumental-variable analyses of alcohol. It offers folate and the MTHFR gene as a case in which genetic findings agreed with trials once intake was known, a model it says does not extend easily to alcohol, and concludes that the approach is fundamentally observational. The PDF prints 'Acknowledgements None' and no funding or conflict-of-interest statement.
